results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body are the calyx, peduncle, and lobes. This information comes from general knowledge in the field of Drosophila neuroscience, as described in the literature (e.g., 2013 review by Aso et al). According to the literature, the lobes are further divided into distinct subdomains. VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila, including the mushroom body, but the specific subdivisions are based on claims made in the literature.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells. According to the VFB database, subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") include [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") types, such as [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Furthermore, Kenyon cells can be categorized into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes. VFB holds extensive data on Kenyon cells, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images, scRNAseq data from [79](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell") records, and transgene expression data from [91](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in Kenyon cell") records, as well as downstream and upstream connectivity classes from [866](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") and [1006](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") records, respectively.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The Drosophila central complex is a complex neural structure in the insect brain that plays a crucial role in spatial memory, navigation, and locomotor control. According to literature (e.g., Wolff et al., 2015; Heinrich et al., 2018), the main components of the Drosophila central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge. 

The ellipsoid body is associated with the processing of visual and spatial information, while the fan-shaped body is involved in the integration of sensory and motor information. The noduli are thought to be involved in the processing of spatial information and the formation of memories, and the protocerebral bridge is associated with the regulation of locomotor activity. 

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of the Drosophila central complex, including 3D reconstructions of the brain and detailed information on the morphology and connectivity of individual neurons. However, the specific functions associated with each component are based on claims made in the literature, rather than VFB database facts. 

From AVAILABLE VFB DATA, we know that VFB contains information on over 23,000 neurons, including those that make up the central complex, as well as data on the expression patterns of various genes in these neurons. However, without more specific queries, it is difficult to provide more detailed information on the functions associated with each component of the central complex.

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, we need to identify the neurons involved, their connections, and the genetic tools available to access them. 

The literature suggests that CO2 avoidance in Drosophila is mediated by a subset of sensory neurons that express the Gr21a and Gr63a receptors (as reported by Jones et al., 2007; and Kwon et al., 2007). These receptors are thought to be responsible for detecting CO2.

According to the literature, the Gr21a and Gr63a expressing neurons project to the antennal lobe, where they synapse with projection neurons that convey the information to higher-order brain regions (as described by  Vosshall and Stocker, 2007). 

To access these neurons genetically, researchers can use the Gal4/UAS system, which allows for targeted expression of transgenes in specific cell types (Brand and Perrimon, 1993). For example, the Gr21a-Gal4 and Gr63a-Gal4 drivers can be used to express transgenes specifically in the CO2-sensitive sensory neurons.

VFB holds data on the expression patterns of various Gal4 drivers, including those used to target CO2-sensitive neurons. However, the specific details of the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila are based on claims from the literature, rather than VFB database facts. 

AVAILABLE VFB DATA indicates that there are numerous Gal4 drivers and other genetic tools available for studying neural circuits in Drosophila, but the exact connections between the neurons involved in CO2 avoidance are not explicitly stated in the VFB database.

In summary, while the literature provides some information on the neurons and genetic tools involved in CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, the VFB database holds data on the expression patterns of Gal4 drivers and other genetic tools, but does not provide a comprehensive description of the neural circuit underlying this behavior.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as reported by Thomas and Wyman (1984). According to the VFB database, there is one giant fiber neuron per hemisphere, with its large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum (Koto et al., 1981; Namiki et al., 2018; Sturner et al., 2025). This neuron can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective (Koto et al., 1981; Power, 1948). The axon enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle (Ito et al., 2014) and descends on the ipsilateral side, in the dorsal cervical fasciculus (Koto et al., 1981; Namiki et al., 2018; Power, 1948). 

In terms of connectivity, the giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons (Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2016). It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget (Matsuo et al., 2016; Namiki et al., 2018). The neuron enters the ventral nerve cord near the dorsal midline and extends posteroventrally to the mesothoracic neuromere, where it turns ventrolaterally and ends abruptly without branching (Koto et al., 1981). In the mesothoracic neuromere, it forms electrical synapses with downstream motor and premotor neurons at the inframedial bridge.

VFB holds a range of data relevant to the giant fiber neuron, including [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes for DNp01. Driver lines for the giant fiber neuron are not specified in the provided evidence, but the available data on transgene expression may be useful for identifying potential driver lines. Relevant publications include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and others cited in the evidence.
